laws.rule: Visitors may drive for up to 12 months on a current full licence; carry an International Driving Permit if the licence has no English translation. Driving unfit through drugs, including prescribed or over-the-counter medicines, carries the same penalties as drink driving.

Controlled drugs, psychoactive substances, offensive weapons, oral tobacco, obscene material, cat and dog fur and counterfeit goods are prohibited imports; importing prohibited goods can mean an unlimited fine and up to 14 years' prison.

items.text: Customs: a visitor may carry a cannabis-based medicinal product only with proof it was lawfully supplied, such as a copy of the latest prescription or a doctor's letter. It should be labelled under the Medicines Act, be no more than a 28-day supply, and stay in the person's possession. If the paperwork can't be checked, the drugs may be seized and the person arrested.
The Misuse of Drugs Act 1976 is the island's main drug law; Isle of Man Customs and Excise guards the border against drugs and asks travellers to cooperate if stopped. Penalty figures were not read.

money-and-cost.currency: Manx pound (equal in value to pound sterling) and pound sterling
money-and-cost.cash_card_notes: Notes: the Isle of Man Government issues its own notes and coins. It states the Manx pound is equal in value to the UK pound but can't be spent outside the Isle of Man. A damaged Manx note can be taken to any Isle of Man Bank branch. Cash declaration: Isle of Man Customs and Excise requires anyone carrying GBP 10,000 or more (or the equivalent in another currency) in or out of the island to declare it, including cash sent by post, courier or freight. GBP 10,000 is about A$19,019 at the RBA rate of 30 October 2026 (A$1 = GBP 0.5258). Form C9011 MAN is available at Ronaldsway Airport and the Sea Terminal. The same page says travellers leaving Great Britain with GBP 10,000 or more for another country must declare it to UK Border Force.
